final_proof:
Work in ZF, without the Axiom of Choice. We use the standard theorem, provable in ZF, that every well-ordered set is order-isomorphic to a unique ordinal.

Let 𝒲 be the set of all pairs (A,R) such that A ⊆ ω and R ⊆ A × A well-orders A. This is a set, since it can be defined by Separation from 𝒫(ω) × 𝒫(ω × ω). For each (A,R) ∈ 𝒲, let ot(A,R) be the unique ordinal order-isomorphic to (A,R). By Replacement,

T = {ot(A,R) : (A,R) ∈ 𝒲}

is a set.

Every member of T is an ordinal, and T is transitive. Indeed, suppose α ∈ T and β < α. There are (A,R) ∈ 𝒲 and an order-isomorphism f:(A,R) → (α,∈). Let

B = f⁻¹[β] = {a ∈ A : f(a) ∈ β}.

Then B ⊆ ω, and the restriction of R to B well-orders B with order type β. Hence β ∈ T. Thus T is a transitive set of ordinals, so T itself is an ordinal. Denote this ordinal by Ω.

We claim that Ω is not countable. More strongly, there is no injection g:Ω → ω. Suppose that such an injection existed. Put C = g[Ω] ⊆ ω and transfer the ordering of Ω to C by defining

g(ξ) S g(η) if and only if ξ ∈ η

for ξ,η < Ω. Because g is injective, this defines a relation S on C, and g is an order-isomorphism from (Ω,∈) onto (C,S). Therefore (C,S) ∈ 𝒲 and ot(C,S) = Ω. By the definition of T, this gives Ω ∈ T = Ω, contradicting the fact that no ordinal belongs to itself. Hence no injection from Ω into ω exists, and Ω is uncountable.

Finally, every proper initial segment of the ordinal Ω has the form

Iα = {ξ ∈ Ω : ξ < α} = α

for some α < Ω. Since α ∈ Ω = T, there are A ⊆ ω and a well-order R of A such that (A,R) has order type α. Thus α is in bijection with a subset of ω and is countable (possibly finite). This last assertion requires no Choice: a subset of ω is already injected into ω; equivalently, if it is infinite, its elements can be enumerated uniquely in increasing order. Therefore every proper initial segment of Ω is countable, whereas Ω itself is uncountable and is well-ordered by ∈. Thus Ω is a minimal uncountable well-ordered set, constructed in ZF without the Axiom of Choice.
